axialTilt.title: Axial tilt & rotation
axialTilt.description: Tilt a planet's rotation axis and watch how sunlight falls on its surface as it spins.

info.title: What is axial tilt?
body: The axial tilt (obliquity) is the angle between a planet's rotation axis and the perpendicular to its orbital plane. Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4°.

Because the axis keeps pointing in the same direction while the planet orbits the Sun, each hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun for one half of the year and away from it for the other – this is what causes the seasons.
Try setting the tilt to 0° (no seasons) or 90° (extreme seasons, like Uranus) and observe how the day/night boundary changes.

solarOrbit.title: Earth's orbit & the habitable zone
solarOrbit.description: Travel through the solar system with real planet positions and see why Earth's near-circular orbit at 1 AU is such a favourable address.

controls.dateOutOfRange: Dates are limited to 1800–2050 (validity range of the JPL orbital elements).

info.title: Why Earth's address matters
info.note: Earth's distance varies only ~5 million km over the year — a remarkably stable energy supply.
info.eccentricNote: With e = 0.3 Earth would swing between 0.70 and 1.30 AU – leaving the habitable zone every year and receiving over three times more sunlight at perihelion than at aphelion.
info.zoneNote: The conservative habitable zone (0.95–1.37 AU) is the region where liquid water can persist on the surface of an Earth-like planet. Earth orbits well inside it; Venus and Mars lie outside.
info.scaleNote: Planet sizes are exaggerated about 1000× for visibility; orbits and positions are to scale (JPL approximate elements, 1800–2050).

habitableZone.title: The habitable zone
habitableZone.description: Explore the narrow ‘Goldilocks’ ring around a star where liquid water can exist – and watch it shift with the star’s type, brightness and age.

planet.habitableHint: Liquid water can persist on the surface.
planet.scorchedHint: Beyond the runaway-greenhouse limit: oceans boil away.
planet.dragHint: Drag the planet to change its distance

evolution.never: Never habitable at {d} AU around a Sun-like star
evolution.note: A Sun-like star brightens by roughly 10 % per billion years, so the habitable zone slowly migrates outward. Earth will reach the inner edge in about one billion years.

info.title: The Goldilocks zone
info.body: Only in a narrow ring around a star can liquid water exist on a planet's surface. For our Sun that ring spans roughly 0.95 to 1.37 AU — and Earth sits comfortably inside it.

physics.title: Physics
physics.zoneLabel: Habitable zone (Kopparapu et al. 2013, conservative limits)
physics.zoneNote: L in solar luminosities. The inner edge is the runaway-greenhouse limit (1.1 S☉), the outer edge the maximum-greenhouse limit (0.53 S☉).
physics.teqNote: d in AU; radiative balance without greenhouse warming (Earth's surface is ≈ 33 K warmer than its equilibrium temperature).
physics.stateNote: The thresholds are the zone edges expressed as temperatures (T_eq depends only on the insolation L/d²). 237 K corresponds to about 0 °C at the surface with an Earth-like greenhouse effect.
physics.evolutionNote: ≈ 0.7 L☉ at birth, 1 L☉ today, ≈ 1.9 L☉ after 10 Gyr – about +10 % per Gyr.
physics.scaleNote: Star and planet sizes are exaggerated for visibility; distances are to scale.

seasons.title: Seasons, axial tilt & day length
seasons.description: Tilt Earth's axis, change its spin and move it around the Sun – and watch seasons, day length and climate zones respond instantly.

presetNotes.noTilt: Without tilt the Sun stands over the equator all year: no seasons, 12-hour days everywhere and permanent climate bands – at the poles the Sun never rises above the horizon.
presetNotes.earth: Earth's 23.4° tilt and 24-hour day produce moderate seasons, day lengths that change gently outside the tropics and a wide range of climate zones – the pattern we know.
presetNotes.uranus: At 90° each pole points straight at the Sun in its summer: half a year of daylight, then half a year of darkness. Over the year the poles receive more energy than the equator – extreme seasons everywhere.
presetNotes.slowRotation: With a 300-hour day every place bakes under the Sun for about 150 hours and then cools for about 150 hours: scorching days and freezing nights.
presetNotes.fastRotation: A 6-hour day would make the Coriolis effect four times stronger: narrower wind belts, far stronger winds and more violent storms – but only mild day–night temperature swings.

readout.dayLength: Day length at the selected latitude

zoneHints.tropical: The Sun passes through the zenith – little seasonal change.
zoneHints.temperate: The Sun is never at the zenith and never stays up or down for a whole day – four seasons.
zoneHints.polar: At least one polar day and one polar night per year.
zoneHints.extreme: Sun at the zenith in summer and polar night in winter.

readout.modelNote: Temperatures are rough estimates from a simple energy-balance model (see “Physics”).

info.title: Why 23.4° matters
info.body: Earth's axis is tilted 23.4°. This creates the seasons, moderate temperatures, and a wide range of climate zones. Without this tilt — or with a much larger one — large parts of the planet would swing between extremes.

physics.title: Physics
physics.declinationLabel: Solar declination (latitude of the subsolar point)
physics.declinationNote: ε = axial tilt, θ = orbit angle counted from the June solstice. The orbit is treated as circular; dates are interpolated between the real equinox and solstice dates.
physics.dayLengthFormula: cos H₀ = −tan φ · tan δ · day = (H₀ / 180°) · P
physics.dayLengthNote: φ = latitude, P = rotation period. If |tan φ · tan δ| ≥ 1 the Sun never sets (polar day) or never rises (polar night).
physics.insolationLabel: Daily mean insolation at the top of the atmosphere
physics.insolationFormula: Q̄ = (S₀ / π) · (H₀ · sin φ · sin δ + cos φ · cos δ · sin H₀)
physics.insolationNote: S₀ = 1361 W/m². Shown by the heat map; it does not depend on the rotation period.
physics.temperatureNote: A = 203.3 W/m², B = 2.09 W/m²/K, C = 3.8 W/m²/K (heat transport), T̄ = 15 °C. Albedo α = 0.31, rising to 0.62 where the annual mean would fall below 0 °C (ice). The seasonal excursion is damped to 60 % to mimic heat storage in the oceans. A rough guide, not a climate model.
physics.swingFormula: ΔT ≈ 14 K · √(P / 24 h) · (sin h_noon − sin h_midnight)
physics.swingNote: h = height of the Sun above the horizon. Longer days let the ground heat up and cool down more; there is no swing during polar day or polar night.
physics.scaleNote: Sizes and distances are not to scale, and Earth's spin is shown far slower than the annual motion would require.
